---
title: "What must be new at prediction time"
---

The earlier page on [populations and samples](../statistical-inference/populations-and-samples.qmd) required an inferential claim to specify the population represented by a sample. Predictive evaluation requires a related decision. We must say which responses were unavailable during fitting and what information is available when those responses are predicted. The [module introduction](index.qmd) describes this choice of held-out unit.

[**Out-of-sample prediction**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html) predicts responses that did not contribute to fitting the model. Out-of-sample can mean a new response row, a new reader, or a new text; the distinction must be stated.

We first reconstruct the Natural Stories measurement process, then distinguish row-, participant-, and story-level prediction targets, and finally specify the information available at prediction time and the linguistic theory that selects the relevant holdout.

## What a Natural Stories row records {#natural-stories-data}

We use the corrected [Natural Stories data](https://github.com/languageMIT/naturalstories), introduced and validated by [Futrell et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-020-09503-7), throughout the first six pages of this unit. The corpus contains English stories enriched for low-frequency syntactic constructions, self-paced reading times, and aligned lexical annotations. One story opens, “If you were to journey to the North of England,” before describing a valley surrounded by high moors. In a self-paced reading trial, a reader reveals this text one region at a time by pressing a button. The latency between two presses is the reading time assigned to the newly revealed word.

The corrected release fixes a one-position displacement: before the correction, a
latency could be attached to the neighboring word rather than the word whose button
press ended that interval. Its preprocessing excludes reader-story passes with fewer
than five correct comprehension answers and reading times outside the release's
100-to-3,000-ms window. These source-defined rules aim to remove poorly attended
passes and implausibly short or long button intervals. They also narrow the target to
retained trials; the notes do not estimate what the excluded responses would have
been.

One retained row records participant `A3QJPB0NZU5PY1` reading *you* at Story 1,
sentence 1, position 2. The observed reading time is 924 ms, so
`log_rt = log(924) = 6.828712`. The predictors have different sources and units:

| Predictor | Source and construction | Unit and interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `word_length` | Number of Unicode characters in the displayed experiment word | Characters, including any characters retained in that displayed token |
| `log_unigram_frequency` | Natural logarithm of the released Google Books unigram count | Log count, not a probability and not a frequency normalized by a common corpus-token denominator |
| `gpt3_surprisal` | For each experiment word, sum the released GPT-3 byte-pair-token `logprob` values, then negate the sum | Released log-probability units; larger values mean that GPT-3 assigned the aligned word less conditional probability in its preceding context |

The checked GPT-3 file names its numerical field `logprob`, but neither that file
nor the accompanying Natural Stories metadata declares a logarithm base. The
course preparation therefore preserves the released values and does not relabel
them as bits or nats. This missing metadata affects the numerical unit, though a
constant change of log base would only rescale this predictor in the linear models
used here.

The **surprisal** of an outcome is the negative logarithm of the probability
assigned to it. Here that probability comes from GPT-3 given the preceding text, so
surprisal describes the model's contextual expectation rather than a participant's
reported expectation. Negating the log probability makes less probable words have
larger values. The missing log base changes the scale, but not this ordering.

This gives the raw-to-modeled ladder used below: a button interval becomes one
participant-by-position `rt_ms`; source filtering retains the trial; a natural log
produces `log_rt`; lexical and contextual annotations are joined by story position;
and complete focal rows enter the regression. The row remains nested within a
participant and a story. No averaging removes that dependence on this page.

The code below filters the corrected Natural Stories source table to complete focal rows and retains the participant, story, word-position, response, and predictor columns. One resulting row is one retained button latency for one reader at one word position. It is a self-paced reading time, not an eye fixation.

```{r}
#| label: natural-targets
#| message: false
#| warning: false

natural_all <- readRDS(
  "data/natural-stories/natural-stories-corrected.rds"
)
natural_all$row_id <- seq_len(nrow(natural_all))

complete_prediction_row <- with(
  natural_all,
  is.finite(log_rt) & is.finite(word_length) &
    is.finite(log_unigram_frequency) & is.finite(gpt3_surprisal)
)

natural <- natural_all[complete_prediction_row, c(
  "row_id", "participant_id", "story_id", "sentence_id",
  "word_position", "word", "word_length", "log_rt",
  "unigram_frequency", "log_unigram_frequency", "gpt3_surprisal"
)]
natural$position_id <- paste(
  natural$story_id, natural$word_position, sep = ":"
)

target_inventory <- data.frame(
  object = c(
    "retained response row", "participant", "story", "sentence",
    "story-position", "participant-story pass"
  ),
  count = c(
    nrow(natural),
    length(unique(natural$participant_id)),
    length(unique(natural$story_id)),
    length(unique(natural$sentence_id)),
    length(unique(natural$position_id)),
    length(unique(paste(
      natural$participant_id, natural$story_id, sep = ":"
    )))
  )
)

participant_means <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ participant_id, data = natural, FUN = mean
)
names(participant_means) <- c("group_id", "mean_log_rt")
participant_means$unit <- "Participant"

story_means <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ story_id, data = natural, FUN = mean
)
names(story_means) <- c("group_id", "mean_log_rt")
story_means$unit <- "Story"

target_variation <- rbind(participant_means, story_means)
target_variation$rank_within_unit <- ave(
  target_variation$mean_log_rt,
  target_variation$unit,
  FUN = function(x) rank(x, ties.method = "first")
)

target_inventory

alignment_exception <- read.csv(
  "data/natural-stories/gpt3-alignment-exception.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
alignment_exception

ggplot2::ggplot(
  target_variation,
  ggplot2::aes(rank_within_unit, mean_log_rt)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7, color = "grey25") + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ unit, scales = "free_x") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Group rank by mean response",
    y = "Mean log reading time"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

The prepared release has `r format(nrow(natural_all), big.mark = ",")` response rows from `r length(unique(natural_all$participant_id))` participants and `r length(unique(natural_all$story_id))` stories. Requiring finite word length, log unigram frequency, and GPT-3 surprisal retains `r format(nrow(natural), big.mark = ",")` rows at `r format(length(unique(natural$position_id)), big.mark = ",")` contextual word positions. The figure shows why a response row, participant, and story are not interchangeable units: the participant and story means vary, but there are only `r nrow(story_means)` story-level values.

Position-based alignment has one documented lexical exception. At Story 2,
position 749, the self-paced reading record and unigram annotation use *peaked*,
while the released GPT-3 input uses *peeked*. The reading time, displayed word,
length, and unigram count therefore concern *peaked*; `gpt3_surprisal` at that
position concerns the model token sequence for *peeked*. We retain the released
position join and expose the mismatch rather than silently treating the strings as
identical.

## Three prediction targets {#three-prediction-targets}

All three procedures used later fit the population regression

$$
\log RT_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1z(L_i)+\beta_2z(F_i)+\beta_3z(S_i)+\epsilon_i,
$$

where $L_i$ is word length, $F_i$ is log unigram frequency, and $S_i$ is released GPT-3 surprisal. What changes is the **prediction unit**, the object excluded from training.

Before the data are observed, $Y_i$ denotes a random log reading time. After the
button interval is recorded, $y_i$ is its realized value. A fitted procedure maps the
available predictor vector $x_i=(L_i,F_i,S_i)$ to the estimate
$\widehat f_{-g}(x_i)$, where $g$ names the held-out row or group. The hat marks an
estimate learned from training data; it is not a new random response.

| target | absent from fitting | still represented in fitting |
|:--|:--|:--|
| new response row | that latency | the reader and story |
| new participant | every latency from that reader | the ten stories |
| omitted enriched story | every latency from that story | the reader population represented by the other stories |

These separations ask different questions. A random row split evaluates another response from the represented collection of readers and stories. A participant split evaluates a reader absent from fitting. A story split evaluates one omitted member of these deliberately enriched texts.

The story target needs especially narrow wording. Recall that
[independence](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent)
requires the joint distribution to factorize. The corpus supplies
`r nrow(story_means)` opportunities to inspect an omitted story, not
`r format(nrow(natural), big.mark = ",")` independent story transfers, because
many response rows belong to the same ten texts. Leave-one-story-out results
consequently describe these ten omissions; they do not estimate performance for
an unrestricted population of English texts.

## The prediction information set

Holding out a group does not by itself determine which information about it may be used. In these analyses, a held-out row keeps its word length, frequency, and surprisal because those predictors are available at prediction time. A held-out participant contributes no reading-time response to fitting. A held-out story contributes its lexical predictors but no response from any of its positions.

The preprocessing rule is part of the information set. Each predictor mean and
[standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd#definition),
which measures spread in the predictor's units, is estimated from training rows
and then applied to test rows. A full-data center would let held-out predictor
values affect the training representation. A separately estimated test center
would place the test observations in a different coordinate system.

The [validation-target specification](index.qmd#validation-target-specification)
keeps five choices separate. In the present sequence, the split unit is a response
row, participant, or story; the score unit is declared on the loss page; lexical
predictors remain available; centers, scales, and coefficients are refit inside the
training fold; and transfer is limited to the represented readers or ten enriched
stories named by the chosen design.

## Theory determines what should be held out

The most demanding split is not automatically the right one. A reading model used for an already represented reader may reasonably target another response row. A claim about transfer across readers requires participant folds. A claim about connected text requires story folds and enough story-level replication to support it.

Successful prediction also does not establish a processing mechanism. Word surprisal can improve a held-out score without showing that readers internally represent the fitted language model's probabilities. Predictive evaluation establishes performance for a stated response, information set, split, and population; the mechanism requires additional evidence.

## Checking the target

1. Which Natural Stories target keeps the same reader and story represented during fitting?
2. What must move together when the target is a reader absent during fitting?
3. Why do the retained response rows not provide that many independent evaluations of an omitted story?
4. Which predictor transformations must be estimated without the held-out responses?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. A random response-row target keeps both its reader and story represented.
2. Every response from that reader must move into the same held-out fold.
3. The rows are repeated measurements within only ten stories, so they do not create
   additional independent story omissions.
4. Predictor centers and standard deviations, together with any response-guided
   transformation or feature choice, must be learned from training rows only.

</details>

## Recap and forward link

1. One row is a retained button latency for one reader and word position.
2. *Out of sample* has no unique group meaning.
3. The information retained about a held-out unit is part of the prediction target.

The [previous page](index.qmd#validation-target-specification) names the full VTS;
the [next page](training-and-test-data.qmd#participant-held-out-validation-target)
implements one participant-held-out split and makes its training-only preprocessing
visible.
